title: When You Find Yourself Far Behind, Reset the Clock
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Drawing on the coaching practice of mentally resetting the score to 0-0 at halftime of a lopsided game, this article argues that reframing a bad outcome as a fresh start restores focus and motivation better than dwelling on the deficit. It explains the underlying psychology: people become demotivated when a gap feels insurmountable, but a mental reset shifts attention from outcome to process, which is where near-term performance actually improves. The piece extends the coaching metaphor directly into workplace settings — trailing teams, missed timelines, blown budgets — arguing the same reset technique clears mental clutter and restores momentum. It ends suggesting that a process-first orientation from the very start might prevent teams from falling behind in the first place.
points: Resetting the score to 0-0 at a natural break point is a coaching technique for interrupting the demotivation caused by a large, seemingly insurmountable deficit.
A mental reset shifts focus from outcome to process, which is specifically where near-term performance gains are made.
The technique transfers directly to workplace settings — missed timelines, blown budgets — not just athletic competition.
A sustained process-first orientation from the outset might prevent the initial collapse the reset technique is designed to recover from.
quotes: When teams get blown away and find themselves in a lopsided game, the best coaches take a pause (halftime) and reset the score to 0-0.
People naturally feel hopeless and become demotivated whenever they are significantly behind in their commitments, goals, and desired outcomes.

Mentally resetting the score or clock allows performers to reframe the situation as a fresh start and to focus their attention on immediate effort and improvement instead of the daunting challenge of catching up.
Going from outcome-focused to process-oriented restores confidence and makes it easier to bounce back from any new obstacle or adversity.
People perform best when they focus on process over outcomes.
